item.title: Underworld links emerge in string of high-profile killings
item.description:
A disturbing pattern has emerged in the capital’s recent crime landscape, with a series of high-profile killings allegedly involving hired professional killers and shooters.
Law enforcement agencies have found evidence suggesting that professional gunmen were used in several recent murders, raising concerns among ordinary residents as well as political leaders and civil society representatives.
According to law enforcement agencies and local sources, some of the killings have links to figures in Dhaka’s underworld. Many of these criminals remained behind bars until around August 5, 2024, before securing bail and being released.
Some are now in hiding, while others have fled the country and taken refuge abroad. From there, law enforcement sources say, they continue to exert influence through killings and extortion.
Those perceived as obstacles to their dominance are allegedly being targeted for elimination.
On November 10 last year, Mamun was killed in front of the National Medical Institute Hospital in Old Dhaka.
The killing was allegedly ordered from Dubai by Emon, known in the criminal underworld as Captain Emon.
Police sources have also confirmed that the order to kill Swachchhasebak Dal leader Azizur Rahman Musabbir on January 7 came from Malaysia.
The alleged mastermind was Dilip alias Dada Binash. Police say Musabbir was killed in Mirpur, Mohakhali, Karwan Bazar and Moghbazar on his orders, while top terrorist Sheikh Mohammad Aslam was allegedly behind the operation. Aslam is known as Sweden Aslam in Dhaka’s criminal underworld.
On April 28, at around 7:45pm, miscreants shot dead top terrorist Khandaker Naim Ahmed Titon in the New Market area.
Titon had been in prison since 2004 and was released on bail on August 13, 2024. His elder brother, Khandaker Sayeed Akhter Ripon, later filed a murder case with New Market police station.
The FIR named top terrorists Pichchi Helal, Badal alias Killer Badal, Shahjahan and Rony alias Vangari Rony as suspects.
According to the FIR, Titon had been involved in a dispute with Pichchi Helal over the lease of a sacrificial animal market.
Titon was also the brother-in-law of Emon. The two had reportedly been involved in a long-standing dispute over arms trading and the expansion of their respective spheres of influence.
A Detective Branch (DB) officer from the DMP’s Ramna division said investigators were examining whether Emon had any involvement in Titon’s murder.
The killing of another top terrorist, Yasin Khan alias Kaillya Palash, was also allegedly ordered from Dubai.
Police sources said fugitive top terrorist Jisan Ahmed Monty had given the order.
On June 12, Kaillya Palash was shot in the head while returning home after prayers near his residence in the Rampura TV Centre area. He died at Evercare Hospital on the night of June 20.
He had been released on bail on May 7, just over a month before the shooting.
In another case, four professional shooters were allegedly hired from Magura and Jhenaidah for Tk25 lakh to kill Kafrul thana Jubo Dal member secretary Hafizul Islam Babu alias Dish Babu.
The four — Chanchal, Jihad Molla, Jiarul Molla and Hasan — were allegedly hired by Hafizur Rahman Hafiz alias CNG Hafiz, joint convener of Kafrul thana Swachchhasebak Dal.
The attack, however, missed its intended target, and Jubo Dal activist Md Yusuf Ali Parvez was killed instead.
Police said they uncovered the plot after arresting and questioning eight people, including the four alleged shooters.
Yusuf was shot dead by armed assailants at around 11pm on July 24 in front of Sher-e-Bangla Primary School in Section 13 of Mirpur.
The name of top terrorist Killer Abbas alias Abbas Ali has also emerged in connection with the killing.
DMP Additional Commissioner (DB) Shafiqul Islam said police were continuing to update their list of professional and hired killers.
“Who follows whom, where instructions are coming from, and who is involved to what extent — the police are working on all these issues,” he said.
Several top terrorists were released from prison on bail in the aftermath of the July uprising.
Killer Abbas was released on bail on August 12, 2024, after being in prison since his arrest on February 14, 2003.
Freedom Rasu was released on August 13. He had been arrested on September 29, 2023.
Emon was released on August 14. Police had arrested him from a flat on Mirza Ghalib Street in Kolkata on December 8, 2007. He was handed over to Bangladesh Police on March 7, 2008, and remained in prison until his release.
Pichchi Helal was released on August 15. He had been arrested on January 12, 2000.
Sweden Aslam was released on September 3. He had been arrested on May 26, 1997.
Freedom Sohel was released on December 19. He had been arrested in 2004 in the Mirzapur area of Tangail.
These top terrorists had been detained at Dhaka Central Jail in Keraniganj and Kashimpur Central Jail in Gazipur.
Jisan, meanwhile, has been living outside the country since 2003.
Crime expert and private university teacher Nasiruddin Samrat said the recent killings showed clear signs of “contract killing”.
He said the main planners were operating behind the scenes, hiring professional killers for large sums of money.
Illegal firearms and techniques to facilitate quick escapes were also being used, he said.
The fact that criminals are carrying out daring attacks in broad daylight or in crowded places and then escaping with ease has raised fresh questions about the overall law and order situation in Dhaka, according to Samrat.
Concern is also growing among residents across the capital.
Rafiqul Islam, a businessman in Farmgate, said the frequency of public killings had made people afraid to leave their homes.
“The attackers are professionals. After receiving the responsibility of killing someone, they complete the job without any hindrance and leave. Where is the security of us ordinary people?” he said.
The recent killings have also caused concern in the political arena.
Those killed or targeted have included political figures, prompting questions about the security of social and political leaders.
Local leaders of major political parties have expressed fears that such crimes could be driven by political motives or attempts to establish influence.
A Jubo Dal leader, speaking to Bangla Tribune on condition of anonymity, said the use of hired criminals showed that criminal networks had become increasingly reckless.
“Those who work in politics, a large section of them are now suffering from insecurity. If this kind of professionalism continues, it will cause a severe deterioration in the law and order situation,” he said.
A senior Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) official said the authorities were treating every recent incident with the highest priority.
“We are identifying not only those who directly participated in the shootings or attacks, but also those at whose direction or with whose money these killings were carried out,” the official said.
He said special operations had begun across the capital to dismantle networks of hired criminal gangs.
Against this backdrop, residents are demanding stronger security measures at key points across the capital.
They have called for increased police patrols, stronger CCTV surveillance and coordinated operations by the Rapid Action Battalion (RAB) and police to recover illegal firearms.
Concerned citizens have also called for the godfathers behind hired criminal networks to be brought to justice and given exemplary punishment.

item.title: Catching time in Gastown
item.description:
Seven summers ago, I was returning home from a business trip to Saskatchewan. On my way back from the Canadian province’s largest city, Saskatoon, I had a several-hour layover in Vancouver. Seizing the opportunity, I roamed around downtown Vancouver and accidentally stumbled upon Gastown—the original 1870s townsite from which the city grew.
As I leisurely strolled along the cobblestone streets of Vancouver's oldest urban district, observing a vibrant mix of trendy restaurants, bars, Victorian-era brick buildings, art galleries, and fashion boutiques, I reached the intersection where Water Street meets Cambie Street. There, I was captivated by an iconic, whistling steam clock standing on the corner—something I had never seen before.
Visitors admiring the beauty of the iconic Gastown Steam Clock, a world-famous landmark located in the historic Gastown district of Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada. Photo: Dhaka Tribune/Collected
The Gastown Steam Clock is one of only seven such functioning clocks in the world. Standing 16 feet tall, it is crafted from gleaming bronze and copper. Its large central whistle sounds the hours with a noise reminiscent of an old locomotive, while four smaller whistles—one at each corner—play the Westminster Quarters every 15 minutes.
Stopping to admire this rare beauty, I listened to it whistle at regular intervals as the mini-chimneys shot out white steam vapor. While the clock partially relies on steam to power its mechanisms, it also utilizes an electric motor.
This close-up selfie captures the Gastown Steam Clock actively blowing steam from its top whistles. Photos: Dhaka Tribune/Collected
Its steam whistles have drawn countless tourists to Gastown for nearly five decades. On the last day of July in 2019, I joined a small crowd gathered at 305 Water Street to watch the whistles go off.
Built by legendary Canadian clockmaker Raymond Saunders in 1977, the clock covers a pre-existing steam vent. Gastown merchants originally commissioned the monument for approximately $58,000.
Raymond Saunders had a display of souvenir Gastown Steam Clocks. Photos: Dhaka Tribune/Collected
True steam clocks—defined as timepieces fully or partially powered by a steam engine and known for emitting steam whistles—are incredibly rare. To be precise, six of the seven running steam clocks globally are the handiwork of Saunders, a famous Canadian horologist.
Three of these seven functioning clocks are located in British Columbia, Canada:
The Gastown Steam Clock: The most famous of his creations.
The Whistler Steam Clock: A smaller, alpine-style steam clock built by Saunders for the resort town of Whistler.
The Port Coquitlam Clock: Another custom-built Saunders creation located in a community square.
The remaining four clocks span the globe:
Otaru, Japan: This massive, 5.5-meter-tall clock was made by Saunders as a gift from Vancouver to Japan. It is currently the largest working steam clock in the world.
Indiana, United States: Another Saunders-made piece located in the American Midwest.
Katoomba, Australia: Unveiled in 2014, Saunders built this clock as a monument to commemorate the region's late-19th-century coal miners.
Jersey, UK: The only clock not built by Saunders. Designed and built by the British clock making company Smith of Derby in 1996, it sits on the Jersey Waterfront in the English Channel. While it historically relied entirely on steam, it was later retrofitted with electrical mechanics for reliability while maintaining its iconic steam display.
This bronze plaque honors the key community contributors who funded the construction of Gastown Steam Clock, including the City of Vancouver, an anonymous contributor, and the Vancouver Gastown Lions Club. Photos: Dhaka Tribune/Collected
The steam that powers the Gastown clock travels through underground pipes connected to a generating plant at West Georgia and Beatty Streets, which provides heat to the downtown core.
After spending nearly half an hour admiring the creation, my only regret was not being able to meet its creator, as I had a flight to catch. I only recently learned through an obituary in the Vancouver Sun that Raymond Saunders passed away in November 2024 at the age of 84.
A close look of Gastown Steam Clock. Photos: Dhaka Tribune/Collected
Saunders worked on virtually every public clock in Vancouver. Born in Courtenay on February 7, 1940, he moved to Vancouver in his teens. His love affair with horology began when his father gave him a box of old alarm clocks to rebuild. After working in the clock department at Woodward’s department store for 11 years, he struck out on his own.
A 1972 photo of horologist Raymond Saunders, a couple of years before he built the Gastown Steam Clock (he started it in 1974 and completed it in 1977). Photos: Dhaka Tribune/Collected
In 1974, a group of local businessmen commissioned him to build the Gastown clock. He accomplished the task over the following three years, sealing his legacy in the clock world. He kept busy restoring timepieces and advising clock collectors right up until his death.
Image features a full view of the Gastown Steam Clock on Water Street in Vancouver, showing its exterior case, internal gears, and the bronze sponsor plaques at the base. Photos: Dhaka Tribune/Collected

item.title: Rifat murder: Minni’s family hopeful of High Court acquittal
item.description:
Paper book preparation is underway for Ayesha Siddika Minni’s appeal against the death sentence handed down by a Barguna court in the 2019 Rifat Sharif murder case.
The High Court accepted Minni’s appeal challenging the 2020 death sentence for hearing, after which work on preparing the paper book began.
However, proceedings have been moving slowly as one of her lawyers, ZI Khan Panna, has been ill.
Minni’s family and lawyers remain hopeful that she will be acquitted by the High Court.
Minni’s lawyer Advocate Mahbubul Bari Aslam (former) told Dhaka Tribune on Friday morning that work on arranging the paper book has been underway since the High Court accepted the appeal for hearing.
“The work is progressing slowly because Minni’s lawyer ZI Khan Panna is ill,” he said.
Aslam said Minni was not directly involved in the murder.
“She tried to save the victim, her husband Rifat, and took him to the hospital. Therefore, we are hopeful that Minni will be acquitted by the High Court,” he said.
Minni is currently serving her sentence at Barisal District Jail.
She was transferred from Kashimpur Jail to Barisal about three months ago following an application citing various health problems.
Senior Jail Superintendent of Barisal Central Jail Subrata Kumar Bala told Dhaka Tribune on Friday morning that Minni is currently at Barisal Jail.
“A clear sign of remorse can be seen in her movements and behaviour. She was young when she made the mistake. Perhaps she has now learned to understand and is able to realize her mistake,” he said.
He said jail is a place for self-correction.
“There is no shortage of our efforts to ensure that all accused correct themselves here, return to normal life after leaving jail and move forward. Minni is also trying to change herself. Perhaps she has realized her mistake,” he said.
Minni’s mother, Jinat Jahan Moni, told Dhaka Tribune on Friday morning that her daughter had been suffering from sinusitis, neck pain, low blood pressure and toothache while in Kashimpur.
“She could not eat properly or sleep. She was always sick. She could not even drink the water at the jail. Later, we applied to have her transferred to Barisal Jail. We met her less than a week ago, and she is better now,” she said.
Jinat said her daughter was young and a victim of her own mistakes and circumstances.
“My daughter was young. She was a victim of her own mistake and circumstances. She was not directly involved in the murder. She also tried to save her husband. We have spent our days shedding tears,” she said.
She expressed hope that the High Court would acquit Minni.
On June 26, 2019, several young men attacked Rifat Sharif with sharp weapons in broad daylight in the College Road area of Barguna.
His wife Minni was with him at the time. Video footage showed her alone attempting to save her husband from the attackers.
The footage also showed several people standing by and watching the attack. After the video spread online, it sparked widespread outrage across the country.
Following the incident, prime accused Sabbir Ahmed Nayan, popularly known as “Nayan Bond,” was killed in an alleged “gunfight” with police.
The investigation took a dramatic turn 21 days after the murder when police arrested Rifat’s wife, Ayesha Siddika Minni.
Before her arrest, Rifat’s father had accused Minni of being involved in his son’s murder.
On September 30, 2020, a court sentenced six people, including Rifat’s wife Ayesha Siddika Minni, to death in the widely discussed Rifat Sharif murder case in Barguna.
Four others were acquitted in the same case.

item.title: Nahid blames Hasina’s Delhi briefing on diplomatic weakness, calls it failure
item.description:
National Citizen Party (NCP) Convenor and Chief Whip of the opposition, Nahid Islam, on Friday said Sheikh Hasina was able to hold a press briefing in Delhi because of the BNP government's failures and diplomatic weakness.
"This is a diplomatic failure of the government. The foreign ministry is trying to earn praise by issuing a press release over fascist Hasina's Delhi briefing. This is mere rhetoric, what we colloquially call empty posturing. Big words are used in the press release, but no diplomatic action is being taken," Nahid told reporters.
He made the comments after visiting a photo exhibition titled "July Still Not Over," organised by Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami on the premises of the opposition leader's official residence.
Nahid said the Awami League had announced the press briefing in advance, and the Delhi government had cooperated with them. “The Indian High Commission should have been summoned and strongly condemned by the government.”
He added that the government should make public what diplomatic measures it plans to take against such incidents in the future.
Alleging that the government is attempting to turn authoritarian, Nahid said if structural reforms are not carried out, the present government too will become autocratic, noting that such a tendency already exists within it.
He said history shows that a "failed Awami League" has repeatedly tried at different times to reassert itself in that mould but has failed in the face of public resistance, citing 1996 as an example. He warned that any fresh attempt now would again meet public resistance.
NCP's chief organiser for the northern region Sarjis Alam, spokesperson Asif Mahmud Shojib Bhuiyan and chief coordinator Nasiruddin Patwary, among other senior leaders, were present during the visit

item.title: Dhaka-Delhi relations face fresh tensions over Hasina
item.description:
The decision to allow Sheikh Hasina to directly interact with journalists in Delhi has created new tensions in Bangladesh-India relations. Although the BNP government had been signalling from the very beginning of its tenure that it wanted to rebuild bilateral relations with India, Wednesday’s interaction has dealt a major blow to that effort.

Several responsible government and diplomatic sources in Bangladesh told Prothom Alo that, two days before Sheikh Hasina’s event in Delhi, Bangladeshi representatives at the policymaking level communicated with a senior representative of the Indian government.

India doesn’t endorse Hasina’s comments: Jaiswal

During their conversation, Bangladesh’s concerns over Sheikh Hasina’s interaction with the media in Delhi were conveyed. In response, the Indian side had assured them that a recorded statement by Sheikh Hasina would be played at the event and that the presence of media personnel would be limited; only members of the organising body would participate. However, ultimately, the assurances were not reflected in the event.

Besides, on 30 July, the central government of India had told the country’s Parliamentary Standing Committee on External Affairs that Sheikh Hasina had not been allowed to conduct political activities from Indian soil. Within a week of that statement, the interaction with journalists was organised.

Bangladesh strongly protested Sheikh Hasina’s interaction in Delhi last Wednesday. The fallout from such tensions and strains in relations between the two close neighbours has spread beyond the political arena into the public sphere as well.

Against such a backdrop, India said yesterday, Friday, that it does not support Sheikh Hasina’s remarks. In response to a question at the Indian Ministry of External Affairs’ regular briefing, ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said, “The Government of India does not endorse anything that was said from that platform, particularly against the duly constituted Government of Bangladesh.”

Bangladesh outraged as India allows Sheikh Hasina to address press in Delhi: Foreign Ministry

Regarding the interaction in Delhi, Bangladesh expressed its anger in a statement issued on Wednesday night, saying, “Bangladesh is outraged that the absconding convicted genocider Sheikh Hasina was allowed this evening to engage in live interaction with the media in New Delhi where she and her henchmen launched venomous vitriol against the State of Bangladesh and her people.”

The government said it had conveyed its concerns apriori to the Indian government about the likely ramifications of the event on the reset of Dhaka-Delhi bilateral relations. Bangladesh deeply regrets that in spite of that the public event was permitted to be held on Indian soil.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs’ statement said, “On a day when the people of Bangladesh are observing the second anniversary of the July Revolution, this interaction by Sheikh Hasina on the Indian soil stands as an affront to the sovereignty of Bangladesh and a grievous insult to the martyrs of the July Revolution.”

Sheikh Hasina's event: Jaiswal says India has no connection

Considering the broader scope of bilateral relations, Indian media outlets also criticised Sheikh Hasina’s remarks in Delhi. The country’s English daily The Indian Express published an editorial yesterday titled “India-Bangladesh ties should be Hasina-proof.” It said, “while a sanctuary offers her (Hasina) a home away from home, turning it into a political platform is problematic.”

A BBC Bangla report from Delhi has raised questions about whether the Indian central government’s approach towards Sheikh Hasina has changed. The report said that Sheikh Hasina herself is one of the major reasons why relations between the two countries have failed to return to a normal rhythm. She has become a source of irritation for Delhi by rejecting all proposals from the Indian government. The BBC Bangla report also questioned whether Sheikh Hasina, once a “trusted friend”, has now become a “burden of discomfort” for India.

New controversy over announcement of return

Sheikh Hasina was convicted of crimes against humanity over the killings during the student-people uprising in 2024. She is a fugitive convict sentenced to death. The activities of her party, the Awami League, have been banned in Bangladesh. Staying in Delhi for the past two years, Sheikh Hasina has at various times sent audio messages through social media. In addition, she has given interviews to various media outlets via email. This was the first time she joined an event in Delhi online and spoke directly.

What analysts say on Hasina’s Delhi press conference and declaration to return home

Sources at the Prime Minister’s Office and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said Sheikh Hasina’s announcement of her return while staying in India has sparked a new controversy. In particular, when she announced her political return to Bangladesh through an interview from Delhi, questions arose among the government’s policymakers as to whether she did so without the consent of the Indian central government. Recently, irritation over the matter has also been expressed at the top levels of the government.

Diplomatic sources in Dhaka and Delhi said Bangladesh has repeatedly asked India to take measures to ensure that Sheikh Hasina cannot conduct anti-Bangladesh activities from Delhi or make attempts to create instability in Bangladesh. As India has not responded to those requests, a crisis of trust has emerged between the two countries.

According to diplomatic analysts, India should remain vigilant to ensure that Sheikh Hasina’s political activities do not damage New Delhi’s relations with the democratically elected government of Tarique Rahman in Bangladesh.

item.title: Jhum cultivators need support
item.description:
Jhum cultivation is an agricultural system that is deeply dependent on nature and the environment. It is not merely a method of farming; it is closely intertwined with the culture, economy and traditions of the indigenous communities in the Chittagong Hill Tracts (CHT). Therefore, jhum cultivators need to be supported and brought under government assistance, including farmer cards and various agricultural incentives, speakers said at a roundtable discussion in Rangamati.

The speakers made the remarks at a roundtable titled “Importance of Jum Cultivation in the Hills: What Needs to Be Done in Light of Reality”, held at Sabarang Restaurant on Rajbari Road in Rangamati town on Thursday afternoon. The discussion was organised jointly by Jabbarang Kalyan Samiti, a non-governmental development organisation, and Prothom Alo.

Dipen Dewan, member of parliament from Rangamati and a guest at the roundtable, said the recognition of jhum cultivation as a form of agriculture should be seriously considered. He said he would discuss with the Ministry of Agriculture and other relevant authorities the possibility of bringing jhum cultivators under farmer cards, government incentives and other agricultural support.

Century-old jhum cultivation in crisis

He also said he would try to place the recommendations emerging from the roundtable before the relevant ministries and policymakers.

Kajol Talukdar, chairman of the Rangamati Hill District Council, said the geographical and ecological characteristics of the CHT are different from those of other parts of the country. In this context, jhum cultivation remains a necessary agricultural system for many hill communities.

“It is therefore not realistic to talk about banning or stopping jhum cultivation. Jhum cultivation will never disappear from the CHT,” he said.

Calling for the recognition of jhum cultivation in the national agricultural policy, Kajol Talukdar said that if the government formally recognises jum production as part of agriculture, jhum cultivators would also be recognised as farmers and become eligible for government support.

He said jhum cultivators are currently deprived of agricultural loans, incentives and other government facilities because they are not formally recognised as farmers. The Rangamati Hill District Council would consider preparing a list of jhum cultivators and exploring the possibility of issuing them special identity cards and providing targeted support, he added.

Dipen Dewan, member of parliament from Rangamati and a guest at the roundtable, said the recognition of jhum cultivation as a form of agriculture should be seriously considered.

Need to change the negative perception

Chief of the Chakma Circle, Debasish Roy, said jhum cultivation should neither be portrayed as the solution to every problem nor blamed for every problem in the hills. However, the long-standing negative perception of jhum needs to change.

He agreed with the demand for recognising jhum cultivation as agriculture, saying such recognition was necessary for jhum cultivators to receive government incentives.

“Jhum cultivators do not practise jhum for pleasure. They do it to earn a livelihood,” he said.

On seed preservation, Debasish Roy said the idea of establishing seed banks was good, but preserving jhum seeds for more than a year is difficult in practice. Therefore, research is needed into appropriate methods for preserving indigenous seeds rather than simply establishing seed banks.

He also called for the establishment of a dedicated research centre on jhum cultivation. Government institutions, district councils, circle authorities, research organisations, NGOs and the media should work together to sustain jhum cultivation, he said.

Professor Khaled Misbahuzzaman of the Institute of Forestry and Environmental Sciences at the University of Chittagong highlighted the importance of jhum cultivation and said it was once a largely self-sufficient agricultural system.

“Meeting the food needs of the family was its primary objective. But the economic reality has changed. People now want to earn more. As a result, they are increasingly turning to hybrid varieties, chemical fertilisers, pesticides and market-oriented crops,” he said.

Explaining how jhum cultivation has changed over time, Professor Misbahuzzaman said a jhum plot was previously left fallow for 20 to 25 years. During this period, soil fertility, microorganisms and biodiversity had enough time to recover naturally.

But the fallow cycle has now become much shorter, reducing the opportunity for the soil and ecosystem to regenerate naturally, he said.

He also observed that the conversion of jhum land into fruit orchards was contributing to an increase in landslides in the hills.

Jhum cultivation in decline, call for incentives

Jhum cultivation is gradually declining in the hills, while interest among the younger generation is also falling.

According to data from the Department of Agricultural Extension in the three hill districts, the area under jhum cultivation has declined by about 2,400 hectares over the past five to 10 years. Jhum cultivation, which once covered 17,723 hectares, is now practised on around 15,326 hectares.

Former member of the National Human Rights Commission Nirupa Dewan called for the establishment of a specialised research centre on jhum cultivation.

Chief of the Chakma Circle, Debashish Roy, said jhum cultivation should neither be portrayed as the solution to every problem nor blamed for every problem in the hills. However, the long-standing negative perception of jhum needs to change.

“Research is needed to understand why the younger generation is moving away from jhum, how they can be reconnected with this traditional agricultural system, and how jhum can be adapted to modern realities and sustained,” she said.

Juwam Lian Amlai, president of the Chittagong Hill Tracts Forest and Land Rights Protection Movement, criticised the tendency to blame jhum cultivation for deforestation and climate change.

He said the Forest Department and various other quarters often blame jhum cultivators for forest destruction and climate change. Instead of simply blaming them, he said, efforts should focus on finding scientifically sound ways to sustain the agricultural system.

Naiupru Marma Mary, a member of the Rangamati Hill District Council, said the disappearance of jhum cultivation would also mean the gradual disappearance of traditional festivals such as the harvest festival, as well as the spirit of mutual cooperation and social values associated with jhum cultivation.

Jhum cultivation on the winding slopes of the hills

Others who spoke at the roundtable included Ashok Kumar Chakma, executive director of Monghar; Bhavatosh Dewan, vice-president of the Chittagong Hill Tracts Headmen Network; Biplab Chakma, head of the Livelihoods and Natural Resources Management Division of UNDP’s SID-CHT; Prabhanshu Tripura, a jhum cultivator from Kaptala Para in Khagrachhari and president of the local PIC; Sucharita Chakma, executive director of Progressive; Dinendra Tripura, executive director of Toymur; Jhum cultivator Phulrani Tripura of Bhangamura Para; and Lalsa Chakma, executive director of Kobidang.

The keynote paper was presented by Partha Shankar Saha, assistant news editor of Prothom Alo. Mathura Bikash Tripura, executive director of Jabbarang Kalyan Samiti, delivered the vote of thanks. The roundtable was moderated by Firoz Chowdhury, assistant editor of Prothom Alo.

item.title: Gas shortage: 4 tips for faster cooking
item.description:
Amid the ongoing gas shortage, a little planning can help you prepare nutritious and delicious meals in much less time.

These practical tips are based on advice from Anika Zaman, a lecturer in the Department of Food and Nutrition at Bangladesh Home Economics College, and culinary expert Sitara Firdous.

Cooking has become something of a race against time these days. As soon as the gas supply returns, there's a rush to finish the day's cooking before it disappears again. Yet working in haste often leads to inefficiency. With a little preparation before the gas comes on, the entire process can become much smoother.

Decide your menu in advance

When the gas supply resumes, many people waste valuable time deciding what to cook first. Prioritise essential items such as rice or flatbread, along with meals for children and older family members.

Quick dishes such as fried or poached eggs, stir-fried vegetables or fried fish can be prepared in between cooking the main meal. This way, you can have two or three dishes ready within a short period.

Save time with smart preparation

Preparing ingredients before the gas returns can significantly reduce both cooking time and gas consumption.

Wash, peel and chop vegetables in advance. If you're cooking meat or fish, remove it from the freezer ahead of time and allow it to defrost naturally.

Marinating meat beforehand helps it cook faster while keeping it tender and flavourful. After washing meat or fish, pat it dry with a clean towel and keep it ready to use.

Prepare ginger and garlic paste in advance, and mix powdered spices with water to make a smooth paste. Soak rice for 20–30 minutes before cooking so it boils more quickly and produces fluffier grains.

You can also boil eggs or potatoes in the same pot while the rice is cooking, saving both time and fuel. If both burners are working, use one to heat water in a kettle. Adding boiling water—not cold water—to curries, soups or lentils speeds up cooking considerably.

Before you start, clear unnecessary utensils from the sink and worktop, and keep the area around the cooker tidy. A clean workspace makes cooking faster and reduces the risk of accidents.

Cook several meals at once

Instead of waiting repeatedly for the gas supply to return, make the most of the available time by preparing meals for two or three sittings at once.

Cook a generous batch of a basic curry base using onions, garlic, ginger and essential spices. When the gas is available again, you can quickly add vegetables, fish or meat to prepare a fresh dish.

One-pot meals such as bhuna khichuri, fried rice or biryani are also practical choices because they combine carbohydrates and protein in a single dish while minimising cooking time.

Similarly, cook enough lentils for several meals and refrigerate them. Before serving, simply temper them with spices for a freshly cooked taste.

Because meat takes longer to cook over a low flame, consider mincing it beforehand. Minced meat cooks much faster and requires considerably less gas.

Store food safely

Low gas pressure often means longer cooking times, which can reduce the nutritional value of food. To save both time and nutrients, use a pressure cooker whenever possible or cook with the lid firmly on the pot.

Avoid reheating cooked food repeatedly, as this increases the risk of food poisoning. Cooked food can generally be stored safely in a standard refrigerator for three to four days. For longer storage, keep it in airtight containers in the freezer.

While it's natural to rush when the gas supply returns, safety should never be compromised. With a little planning and an organised approach, you can prepare healthy meals quickly and safely, even during the ongoing gas shortage.

item.title: Concerns persist over unrecovered looted weapons and fugitive prisoners
item.description:
A shotgun was found in a fisherman’s net while he was fishing in Singarpur of Araihazar, Narayanganj, on Monday. Police later confirmed through registration records that the firearm was among those looted from Araihazar police station during the July uprising.

The incident has once again highlighted that a portion of the firearms and ammunition looted from police stations and prisons during the uprising remains unrecovered. It has also drawn attention to the fact that hundreds of prisoners who escaped from jails at the time are yet to be arrested.

Senior police officials say looted firearms have ended up in the hands of criminals and are being used in various crimes. There have also been cases of police personnel being involved in the sale of looted weapons. Among the escaped prisoners are several death-row convicts and militants, raising concerns over the country’s overall law and order situation.

According to Police Headquarters data, following the fall of the Awami League government on 5 August 2024, police stations, outposts, police boxes and other police facilities across the country were attacked, vandalised and set on fire. A total of 5,763 firearms and 652,008 rounds of ammunition were looted.

The looted weapons included rifles, submachine guns, light machine guns, pistols, shotguns and gas guns, as well as tear-gas launchers, shells and sprays, sound grenades, colour-smoke grenades, stun grenades and ammunition of various calibres.

A joint operation to recover the looted weapons and ammunition began within a month, on 4 September 2024. As of 5 July this year, 4,445 firearms and 394,869 rounds of ammunition had been recovered. This means 1,318 firearms and 257,139 rounds of ammunition were still unaccounted for as of that date.

Hundreds of prisoners still at large

Before and after the fall of the Awami League government, unrest broke out in several prisons during the July uprising. According to the Department of Prisons, 2,240 prisoners escaped from different jails during that period.

A total of 94 shotguns and Chinese rifles were also looted from prisons. Of the escaped prisoners, 683 are yet to be arrested. Twenty of the shotguns and Chinese rifles looted from prisons also remain unrecovered.

When asked, Brigadier General Syed Md. Motahar Hossain, Inspector General of Prisons, told Prothom Alo that among the unrecovered prisoners, 69 are considered high-risk, including 60 death-row convicts and nine militants.

He said some of the looted Chinese rifles and shotguns have also not been recovered. The Rapid Action Battalion (RAB) and police continue to arrest convicted prisoners from time to time, he said, adding that there is no immediate risk to prison security. However, he believes the overall law and order situation in the country faces a mild security risk.

Police constable involved in sale of looted gun

On 3 March last year, a pistol was recovered from the scene after two people were killed in a lynching in Satkania, Chattogram. Police said the pistol had been looted from Kotwali police station of Chattogram Metropolitan Police.

One of the men killed, Nezam Uddin, had allegedly fired the weapon before the mob attack, injuring four people, including a local shopkeeper.

Police later found that Constable Md Riyad, who was then posted in Chandpur, was involved in the sale of the weapon. Riyad, a resident of Satkania, and five others were arrested from Patenga and Bakalia in Chattogram on 21 March. Police recovered a foreign-made pistol and seven rounds of ammunition from them.

Police said an initial investigation found that the pistol had also been looted from Lohagara police station. Riyad was suspended following his arrest. He and two associates later gave confessional statements before a Chattogram court.

On 19 June that year, police arrested Saidur Rahman Masum alias Red Masum, 28, from the Jelepara-Rani Rashmoni Ghat area of Chattogram. A pistol and four rounds of ammunition were recovered from him.

According to CMP, Masum was the leader of a major criminal gang in the city. The pistol recovered from him had been looted from Pahartali police station. Police said he and his associates had used the weapon in snatching, robbery and other crimes.

Additionally, police have arrested several criminals on charges of committing murders and extorting money using firearms looted from police stations, reports of which have appeared in the media.

Additional Inspector General of Police (Crime and Operations) Khondoker Rafiqul Islam told Prothom Alo that police operations to recover looted firearms and ammunition are continuing.

Although progress is slow, some looted police weapons are being recovered from time to time. However, he does not believe this poses a threat of deterioration to the law and order situation.

item.title: No jobs despite having degree: Anxiety in millions of unemployed graduate
item.description:
“Where do you see yourself in five years?” When an interview board asks the question, the candidate gives a brief reply: “Sir, I would be happy if I could simply pay next month’s mess rent for now.”

Although the joke has become popular on social media, it reflects the grim reality facing millions of highly educated unemployed people in the country.

After earning a degree, young people now worry more about meeting their monthly living expenses than pursuing long-term professional ambitions.

The latest Labour Force Survey by the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) provides statistical evidence of this reality.

According to the data, the unemployment rate among highly educated people or university graduates currently stands at 13.54 per cent, the highest among all educational groups. In total, around 885,000 graduates in the country remain unemployed.

By contrast, the unemployment rate among people with no formal education is only 1.25 per cent. In other words, the higher the level of formal education in Bangladesh, the greater the risk of remaining unemployed.

These statistics are not merely figures on paper; they are putting increasing pressure on people’s everyday lives. Take Asif, a former student of Jagannath University, who lives in a mess in Narinda, Old Dhaka.

Two years after completing his graduation, he still spends each day worrying about finding a job and paying his mess rent. In another part of Dhaka, Tanvir, who lives in a mess in Rajabazar, struggles to cover commuting costs and other essential daily expenses.

Meanwhile, Rony travels between Rangpur and Dhaka to sit for recruitment examinations while staying in a mess in Rangpur.

He is already two months behind on his mess rent, and the local grocery shopkeeper has added his name to the credit ledger.

Experts say these three young men represent only a fraction of the millions of unemployed youths in the country.

Although educational institutions produce an average of around 700,000 graduates every year, the formal job market creates only about 300,000 jobs.

An analysis of statistics from the Bangladesh Public Service Commission (BPSC) shows that candidates generally take three to five years to progress from the preliminary examination to final recruitment recommendations for the Bangladesh Civil Service (BCS) or combined bank recruitment.

This prolonged wait also creates age and experience barriers to entering the private sector.

Professor Ridhwanul Haq of the Institute of Business Administration (IBA) at the University of Dhaka has identified the mismatch between educational qualifications and labour-market demands as one of the major problems.

He said, “In the era of AI, formal employment opportunities will shrink in various fields, from media to accounting. However, opportunities for technically skilled workers will remain, and demand for such skills will increase significantly in the future. Therefore, we must bring technical education in the country up to international standards and increase the use of technology.”

At the same time, the country needs to take immediate steps to address the crisis facing young people.

Students in Bangladesh often spend three to four years after graduation preparing solely for examinations for specific government or major corporate jobs.

To overcome this rigidity, they should engage in internships, part-time employment or skill-based projects while studying or immediately after graduation.

Starting any kind of work can help young people overcome their reluctance to enter the workforce and may eventually open the door to a broader career.

Data from the International Labour Organization (ILO) and other global indicators show that the unemployment rate among young people aged 18 to 24 in Bangladesh stands at 9.39 per cent.

Economists at the Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD) and the World Bank say that a lack of appropriate skills leaves billions of dollars’ worth of human resources underutilised every year.

As highly educated young people remain unemployed for prolonged periods, Bangladesh is losing the benefits of its crucial “demographic dividend”, with the estimated loss amounting to several billion dollars a year in terms of national GDP growth.

Career experts say discussions on policy reforms and changes to the education curriculum may take years, but thousands of young people across the country are currently spending their days struggling simply to survive each month.

As they try to balance mess rent with recruitment examination application fees, a significant portion of an entire generation’s talent and youth remains trapped in a cycle of uncertainty.

item.title: Gold price raised to Tk234,800 per bhori
item.description:
The Bangladesh Jewellers Association (Bajus) has raised the price of gold in the local market, with the new rates taking effect from 10am on Saturday.
The decision was made at a meeting of Bajus's Standing Committee on Pricing and Price Monitoring earlier in the day.
According to a Bajus notification, the price of 22-carat hallmarked gold has been set at Tk20,065 per gram, including VAT. Accordingly, the price of one bhori (11.664 grams) stands at around Tk234,800, excluding labour charges, which will vary depending on the design.
The price of 21-carat hallmarked gold has been set at Tk19,165 per gram, while 18-carat gold will cost Tk16,455 per gram. The price of traditional gold has been fixed at Tk13,445 per gram.
Bajus has also revised the prices of silver ornaments.
According to the new rates, 22-carat hallmarked silver will cost Tk420 per gram, including VAT, while 21-carat and 18-carat silver will cost Tk400 and Tk345 per gram, respectively. Traditional silver has been priced at Tk260 per gram.
Bajus said VAT is already included in the fixed selling prices, meaning jewellers cannot charge customers additional VAT when selling gold or silver ornaments.
However, labour charges will apply depending on the design and type of jewellery.
The association said its existing rules regarding the exchange and purchase of gold and silver jewellery will remain in effect, apart from the fixed VAT, labour and stone charges.
The new prices will remain effective at all jewellery shops across the country until further notice, Bajus said.
The notification was signed by Dr Dewan Aminul Islam Shaheen, chairman of Bajus's Standing Committee on Pricing and Price Monitoring.
Bajus regularly adjusts gold prices based on international and domestic market rates, the price of pure gold and overall market conditions.

item.title: Rebuilding lives after disaster
item.description:
The government’s decision to provide new homes to 100 flood-affected families is a commendable initiative. For the families that lost their homes to the recent floods, the construction of disaster-tolerant houses on their own land offers not only shelter but also a measure of stability at a time when their lives have been severely disrupted.
The disaster-tolerant design of the homes is particularly welcome, and such gestures should absolutely be extended to more families who remain vulnerable after disasters.
However, rehabilitation must be accompanied by a stronger emphasis on preparedness: Bangladesh’s vulnerability to floods is well established, and increasingly erratic weather patterns and intense rainfall make it all the more important to anticipate disasters rather than simply respond to them.
Relief and reconstruction are essential, but a genuinely resilient disaster-management system must aim to reduce the scale of damage in the first place.
This requires sustained investment in flood-control infrastructure, including stronger embankments, drainage systems, and waterways. Early-warning systems must be made more effective and accessible -- particularly in remote communities, where timely information can save lives.
Local administrations should also have adequate resources, trained personnel, and clear contingency plans to coordinate evacuations, shelters, rescue operations, and relief distribution before emergencies escalate.
Equally important is ensuring that reconstruction is guided by risk assessments. Houses, roads, schools, and other essential infrastructure in flood-prone areas should be built or upgraded to withstand recurring hazards rather than reconstructed in ways that leave communities exposed to the next disaster.
The government undoubtedly deserves credit for helping these 100 families rebuild their lives, but this should be part of a broader, sustained commitment to disaster resilience. More such housing initiatives should follow, alongside stronger preparedness measures.
Only then can Bangladesh move from repeatedly recovering from floods to substantially reducing their human and economic toll.

item.title: Fixing the media landscape
item.description:
Information and Broadcasting Minister Zahir Uddin Swapon is right to identify misinformation as the biggest challenge facing journalism today, in addition to objective journalism slowly fading.
With that said, acknowledging the problem is only the beginning, and is unhelpful without actions taken.
We are now operating in a digital environment where falsehoods spread faster than verified information, where rumours routinely outpace official statements, and where manipulated content can destabilize public behaviour within minutes.
As such, Bangladesh cannot continue responding to misinformation only after it has done its damage, and it cannot expect objective journalism without the right support and ecosystem to allow such journalism to thrive.
Millions of Bangladeshis consume news primarily through social media, often without the skills to distinguish verified reporting from manipulated content. Schools, community institutions, and media outlets must help citizens learn how to evaluate sources and avoid spreading unverified claims, while the government must do its part in ensuring that these do not get drowned out by the noise of disinformation campaigns.
The media landscape in Bangladesh has needed reform for some time now, and in order to bring forth good journalism, the government has to play a major part.
Of course, media institutions must do their due diligence as well, and must operate with the highest standards possible. Nevertheless, while fact‑checking and responsible reporting are more essential than ever in an era where speed often eclipses accuracy, resisting the temptation to chase viral content only happens when there are sufficient resources for media agencies to not need to resort to such means.
Misinformation is indeed one of our biggest challenges in the media, as is the fight for objectivity. To combat it, and correct the course of journalism in this country, will require substantial effort and support from the authorities. Without it, the challenge will only grow.

item.title: My cross-border healthcare experience
item.description:
On December 30, 2025, while travelling to my office, as on any other working day, I became the victim of a road accident in Dhaka which severely injured my left knee. Later, following the advice of colleagues, well-wishers, and family members, I decided to seek advanced medical treatment in India.
My consultation with Dr Atul Srivastava was one of the most reassuring moments of my treatment journey. He listened patiently to my concerns, carefully reviewed the required medical examinations, and recommended ligament reconstruction surgery. Under his supervision, the surgery was successfully completed. Beyond being a highly skilled surgeon, I found him to be a compassionate and empathetic human being.
Even after the surgery, he continued to provide regular guidance, precautions, and rehabilitation-related advice, all of which significantly contributed to my recovery. What stood out most was the importance he placed not only on medical treatment, but also on my mental well-being, anxieties, and confidence.
This patient-centred approach was clearly reflected in both his behaviour and medical practice.
On April 8, I was admitted to Narayana Multispecialty Hospital, Howrah. From the admission process to the preparation for surgery, every step was highly organized, modern, and professional. One aspect that particularly impressed me was the comprehensive pre-operative assessment conducted by the anesthesiology team before the hospital admission. In many hospitals across South Asia, patients often experience admission procedures where administrative and financial formalities receive greater attention than patient communication. In contrast, this hospital demonstrated an impressive blend of professionalism, empathy, and patient-centred care.
The moments before surgery, especially during the administration of anesthesia, were also a remarkable experience for me. The anesthesiologist explained the entire procedure in simple language, behaved with exceptional warmth, and paid equal attention to my emotional comfort.
Before administering the anesthesia, consent was sought, every step was explained, and reassuring words helped replace anxiety with confidence. As a result, I experienced remarkably little fear during the process.
This experience showed me how important humane behavior from healthcare professionals can be in building a patient’s confidence and mental preparedness.
The hospital’s ward management, nursing support, cleanliness, and overall environment were all of a high standard. The staff members were consistently courteous, compassionate, and responsible in their dealings with patients.
Perhaps the most exceptional part of my experience occurred on May 7. At the time, I was at my home in Bangladesh. Suddenly, I experienced severe pain and some complications in my leg. I contacted Dr Atul Srivastava over the phone. Despite the late hour, he listened patiently to my concerns and asked me to send my discharge summary, latest prescription, and photographs of the affected area. After reviewing everything, he promptly provided the necessary advice and prescribed medication for one month.
In today’s world, receiving such attention, responsibility, and compassion from an internationally respected specialist is truly rare. To me, this was not merely a treatment experience; rather, it was a living example of a doctor’s sense of responsibility and humanity toward a patient.
My treatment journey reinforced one important lesson: The quality of modern healthcare does not depend solely on advanced technology or surgical expertise. Patient-centred behaviour, effective communication, emotional support, and proper post-treatment follow-up are equally important.
Compassionate behavior, clear explanations of medical procedures, and the accessibility of doctors during times of need can often provide patients with greater comfort and confidence than medicine itself.
Patients often remember not only the treatment they receive, but also how they are treated as human beings during vulnerable moments of their lives.
Looking back on my treatment journey, I realized that certain patient-centred approaches could play an important role in further enhancing healthcare services in Bangladesh.
These include comprehensive pre-admission assessment, clear communication regarding treatment procedures, psychological preparation of patients, organized ward management, personalized nutrition, and structured post-operative follow-up.
None of these require extraordinary technology; rather, they reflect a culture of patient-centred healthcare.
At the same time, alongside professional expertise, doctors, nurses, and support staff should receive further training and awareness on sincere communication, empathetic behaviour, and emotional support for patients.
Treatment is not only about physical recovery; it is also deeply connected to mental strength and human reassurance.
Bangladesh's healthcare sector has made remarkable progress over the past decades. The country is home to many highly competent physicians, dedicated healthcare professionals, and increasingly modern medical facilities.
Building further on these strengths through patient-centred management, humane behaviour, and compassionate care can help elevate healthcare services to even higher international standards.
My cross-border treatment journey reminded me that the true measure of a hospital is not defined solely by its infrastructure or technology, but by the dignity, respect, empathy, and confidence it offers every patient.
Ruhul Kuddus is involved with education program management and development work.

item.title: Hate should never replace facts
item.description:
The Rohingya are one of the world's most persecuted and stateless peoples. They were forced to flee to many countries because of genocide, violence, mass killings, and the burning of their homes and belongings. Today, the majority of the Rohingya have taken shelter in neighbouring countries, especially Bangladesh which currently hosts over one million of them.
"We are struggling to gain recognition in the land where we were born. Our demands are our denied citizenship rights and the right to return to our original homeland. Instead, we are facing widespread hate speech everywhere," said Khin Khin Nu, a female citizen journalist from Myanmar.
Over the past few decades, the Myanmar military has launched several hate campaigns and propaganda against the Rohingya. This campaign spread throughout the country, and civilians used slurs such as "Bengali," "kalar," "dogs," and many other dehumanizing terms.
I have witnessed a similarly alarming rise in online hate campaigns targeting the Rohingya in Malaysia. What concerns me most is not criticism based on evidence, but the normalization of collective hatred built on misinformation, stereotypes, and false narratives.
For the past two months, I have spent a great deal of time arguing and responding to comments from many Malaysians on Facebook. I always ask the same simple question: What have the Rohingya, as a community, done to deserve this level of hatred? Please provide solid evidence.
Most of the answers I receive are that some Rohingya spit betel nut saliva, throw garbage on the streets, beg in public, or have poor manners. But this is a traumatized community that has grown up under genocide, repeated oppression, without proper education, and without the opportunity to grow up in stable families with proper parenting.
Even if such incidents happen, how can they justify hatred against an entire ethnic community? Every society has individuals who behave poorly. We do not judge millions of people by the actions of a few.
One of the most common misconceptions is that Malaysia financially supports the Rohingya. This is simply not true. Refugees registered with UNHCR receive refugee documentation from the agency, and UNHCR covers part of certain medical expenses.
The rest of their lives -- including rent, food, clothing, education, transportation, and most healthcare costs -- are paid for by the refugees themselves. They survive through their own hard work, often in difficult and low-paid jobs.
Malaysia has welcomed migrant workers from many countries to contribute to its economy, and many Rohingya are also part of that workforce. They are not asking the Malaysian government to provide them with a comfortable life or special rights. They simply want the opportunity to earn an honest living while waiting for a durable solution, whether that is returning to their homeland, resettlement in a third country, or at least access to basic education.
Many Rohingya have already been resettled in countries such as Canada, the United States, Australia, and New Zealand. Those who remain in Malaysia are not there because they want to settle permanently. Most are simply waiting for the opportunity to rebuild their lives elsewhere through legal resettlement.
In an interview with DVB News, Rohingya activist Farooq said:
"We fled from genocide. We are not coming here (Malaysia) to take over jobs, take land, or demand rights. We are here just to survive and stay safe."
But today, many Malaysians are being presented with a very different image through organized online hate campaigns. False information has played a major role in fueling public hostility.
In Kuala Lumpur, there have reportedly been cases where people from Bangladesh, India, Myanmar, and other countries pretended to be Rohingya in the hope of obtaining refugee resettlement opportunities. Yet when these individuals are involved in misconduct, the blame is often placed on the entire Rohingya community.
There have also been cases where people from other countries falsely identified themselves as Rohingya and married Malay women. After obtaining property or financial benefits, they reportedly returned to their own countries. But the Rohingya do not have a country to return to. They cannot simply go back because they have no recognized nationality, passport, or visa. Many people fail to understand this important difference.
I have also seen AI-generated posters and misleading social media posts portraying the Rohingya as criminals. Such content is designed to provoke anger rather than encourage understanding. If an individual commits a crime, that person should be held accountable. Justice should always be individual, never collective.
From what I have observed online, many of the people actively participating in these hate campaigns identify themselves as Malaysians, but they are not ethnic Malays. Many appear to come from Indian, Indonesian, Rakhine, Nepali, Sri Lankan, Filipino, or other backgrounds.
I have also seen the word "kalar" being used in posters circulating in Malaysia. This slur has been widely used in Myanmar for decades by some Burmese and Rakhine people against the Rohingya. Seeing the same language appear in Malaysian hate campaigns raises serious concerns that Burmese and Rakhine actors may also be involved.
Regardless of who is involved, organized hate speech against an entire refugee community is unacceptable.
Criticism based on facts is legitimate. Every community has individuals who break the law, and they should face justice. But blaming an entire ethnic group for the actions of a few is discrimination, not accountability.
The Rohingya have already lost their homes, their citizenship, and their basic rights. They should not also become the targets of organized hatred based on misinformation. They are victims of an ongoing genocide and persecution and deserve stronger protection and security measures from the international community and the United Nations.
I respectfully call on the international community and Meta to investigate the widespread online hate speech directed at the Rohingya and to enforce its community standards consistently. At the same time, I encourage everyone to verify information before sharing it. Facts should guide our opinions -- not prejudice, misinformation, or collective blame.
We do not want to live as refugees, asylum seekers, or displaced people forever. Let us return to our homeland with our citizenship and rights. Otherwise, if the world has no place for us, then throw us into the Pacific Ocean altogether.
Ahtaram Shin is a Rohingya independent journalist and freelancer.
